## TL;DR

Release emails are in. A project with an email provider can turn on `[release.email]` (Settings → General → Release emails, or `repoos.toml`) and each stable cut emails its recipients once, with the version, date, release notes, known issues and links. By default the email waits until GitHub serves the release with its assets. Prereleases are skipped unless a toggle is on. Sends are recorded per version and per recipient, so a restart or retry does not mail anyone twice. This round I closed the review-pass-2 findings: the mid-send restart window, the probe's handling of non-JSON answers, the preview route's error handling, the clipped Settings label, and the `[release.email]` without `[release]` case. Nothing was sent to a real address; tests use a fake provider and a fake fetch.

## Work and rationale

The send path reuses `sendEmail` in `src/server/email.ts`, the same function login codes use, so there is one Resend client and one From header. The release side lives in `src/server/release-email.ts`: the renderer (subject, HTML, plain-text alternative, all user text escaped), the publish probe, the send loop and the record store (`release-emails.json`, keyed by version).

Publish detection polls the public GitHub releases-by-tag endpoint with plain `fetch`, no auth and no client library. A release counts as published when it is not a draft and has at least one asset. The first look decides the fallback: if GitHub cannot be reached at all, the email goes out at the tag and the record says so. A 404 or an error answer keeps waiting with backoff until the timeout. A timeout records a failure with a Resend button rather than sending early. The rule I held to is that a failure to detect never fails the release. Every path runs under `startCutReleaseEmail`, which is detached from the cut.

Idempotency lives in the record. Each accepted recipient is written to `sentTo` before the next send, so a crash after recipient 1 leaves recipient 1 marked as sent. A `pending` record with no waiter in this process reads as failed with a reason and a Resend button, rather than silently re-running. Resend sends only to recipients not yet in `sentTo`, and it refuses while a send for the same version is in flight. The preview endpoint renders the message with no send.

Surfacing: the Releases page shows the email state on its own card with Preview and Resend. Missing provider and send failures also go to the bell, and a later successful send clears that notice. The Settings control is a select labelled "When published" / "When tagged" (shortened from the longer labels that clipped), with a real example address as the recipient placeholder. The config loader warns when `[release.email]` is enabled but `[release] enabled` is not true, because a cut is the only trigger.

Docs: `docs/releases.md` and `user-docs/configuration.md` cover enabling it, the provider prerequisite, the published-versus-tagged choice, the timeout, the preview and Resend, and what the email contains.

## Approaches tried

In an earlier round the per-recipient write sat after the send loop. Review pass 2 pointed out that a restart mid-loop would re-mail the early recipients. The fix writes inside the loop, next to each accepted send. That is one write per recipient, which is cheap at team sizes and is the only ordering that survives a crash between two sends.

For the probe, the earlier code let the whole fetch-and-parse block fall under the "unreachable" branch. A captive portal that answers 200 with HTML would then have triggered the tag fallback on the first look. It is now split: only the `fetch` call maps to unreachable, and a body that is not JSON is an HTTP-level answer that keeps the wait going.

I considered a git hook for the tag and rejected it, as the spec says: a local hook fires before CI has published, so the email would name a download that does not exist yet.

The longer Settings option text was clipped in the capture, so it is now "When published" / "When tagged".

## Challenges and blockers

The check that had failed before this round listed four tests: `git-ref-watcher` (a linked-worktree case), `agent-start-host-pressure`, `agent-review` (partial output without a verdict) and `debugger-integration`. None touch release code, and all 30 of those tests pass when run together. The check I ran this round failed on one test, `serve-reaper`'s orphaned-root sweep case. That test waits a fixed 200 ms for a child process to start, then expects the sweep to find it. Under load the child can still be starting, so the sweep finds nothing. Per the repo's rule to remove a timing race rather than reconcile it, the test now waits for the child to print a ready line before it deletes the root. The file passed three runs in a row. I did not change the other four tests; they pass in isolation and did not fail in this round's run.

The final scoped `repoos check --changed main` passed: 531 test files and 7462 tests, with one skipped.

The branch is behind main, so `git diff main` shows other tasks' report files as deleted. That is main's progress, not this branch's change, and close-out builds from current main.

The Settings placement differs from the spec's wording, which says "under Releases". It lives in Settings → General → Release emails, which keeps every `release.email.*` key in one section. I took that as acceptable and flag it for sign-off.

I cannot run a real send here, and I did not. Whether the Resend key works, and whether a real inbox gets the message, is for a human with the project's key to verify. The Releases card's failed and pending states are only covered by tests; the screenshot shows the off state.

## Key learnings

A review finding names one line, but its class usually repeats. The restart-ordering bug was about any side effect followed by a delayed write, so I checked the Resend path too, and it shares the same sender, so the fix covers both.

Error classification should follow what failed, not where the code sits. Putting `res.json()` in the network `try` made a bad body look like a dead network. Keep "could not reach" for the request itself.

A route that does work before its `try` leaks a generic 500 past its own error shape. Keep the whole handler inside the guard.

Shots need a stable hook. The Settings section has `data-settings-section`, which survives copy changes, while the Releases card only renders once a release state loads, so a shot of it depends on the preview's release history.

A fixed sleep is a race that shows up only under load. The sweep test passed alone and failed in the full run until it waited on a signal from the child.

Follow-ups filed for what does not belong here: #1092 the `repoos release email --preview` CLI subcommand (the route is reachable through `repoos api` today), #1093 a send-to-self test through the real sender, and #1094 rich templates with unsubscribe and non-GitHub links.
